title: Localizations of N-1 and N-2 domains
statement: Let $R$ be an integral domain with field of fractions $K$ and $S\subseteq R$ a multiplicative subset ($1\in S$, $st\in S$ for $s,t\in S$) with $0\notin S$, and let $S^{-1}R$ be the localization [def-weil-pbc-module-localization]. Then $S^{-1}R$ is an integral domain, and the map $S^{-1}R\to K$, $r/s\mapsto r/s$, is injective and identifies $K$ with the field of fractions of $S^{-1}R$. Moreover: (1) if $R$ is N-1 [def-weil-pbc-japanese-domain], then $S^{-1}R$ is N-1; (2) if $R$ is N-2 [def-weil-pbc-japanese-domain], then $S^{-1}R$ is N-2.

proof.text: For any field $L$ containing $K$, every $s\in S$ has nonzero image in $L$, hence is invertible. Consequently the localization $S^{-1}L$ is identified with $L$ by $b/s\mapsto b s^{-1}$, with inverse $b\mapsto b/1$. Let $C_L$ be the integral closure of $R$ in $L$. Applying [lem-weil-pbc-integral-closure-commutes-localization] to $R\to L$ identifies the integral closure of $S^{-1}R$ in $L$ with the image of $S^{-1}C_L$.

source.place: Tag 032G, lemma-localize-N, proof, using Tag 0307, lemma-integral-closure-localize

proof.text: If $C_L$ is generated as an $R$-module by $c_1,\ldots,c_n$, write any $c\in C_L$ as $\sum_i r_i c_i$. Then $c/s=\sum_i(r_i/s)(c_i/1)$ in $S^{-1}C_L$. Hence $c_1/1,\ldots,c_n/1$ generate that localization, and therefore its identified integral closure, as an $S^{-1}R$-module. This follows directly from [def-weil-finitely-generated-module] and the localization operations.

proof.text: If $R$ is N-1, use $L=K$: the definition [def-weil-pbc-japanese-domain] makes $C_K$ finite, so the preceding steps prove N-1 for $S^{-1}R$. If $R$ is N-2, take any finite field extension $L/K$; the same definition makes $C_L$ finite. Since the fraction field remains $K$, these are precisely all the extensions required for N-2 of $S^{-1}R$.
